---
title: "Where does the wing actually stall?"
---

{{< include _model.qmd >}}

The lift curve taken out to 24° rather than the 16° the stall search used, at the
three speeds this chapter trims at, to establish whether it has one peak or more
than one.

::: {.callout-note}
## Assumed
Nothing new. This is the chapter's own `polars()` read over a wider range of
angle than any entry has asked it for before.
:::

```{python}
a = np.linspace(0, 24, 241)
curves = {V: np.array(polars(a, V=V)["CL"]) for V in [3.73, 3.96, 4.46]}


def peaks(CL):
    """Every local maximum, in order. The first one is the stall."""
    return [i for i in range(1, len(CL) - 1)
            if CL[i] >= CL[i - 1] and CL[i] > CL[i + 1]]


rows = []
for V, CL in curves.items():
    p = peaks(CL)
    g = int(np.argmax(CL[a <= 16]))          # what a global search over 0-16 finds
    rows.append((V, a[p[0]], CL[p[0]], a[g], CL[a <= 16][g], len(p)))
worst = max(r[3] - r[1] for r in rows)
```

**Answer.** At `{python} f"{rows[0][0]:.2f}"`–`{python} f"{rows[-1][0]:.2f}"` m/s
the wing stalls between `{python} f"{min(r[1] for r in rows):.1f}"`° and
`{python} f"{max(r[1] for r in rows):.1f}"`°. There is exactly one peak, but the
curve does not simply fall away after it: lift dips to about 13°, then climbs
steadily again and is still rising at 24°, by then well above anything it
reached before the stall (@fig-doublepeak). That renewed rise is deep post-stall
behaviour, outside the attached-flow regime the section data represents, and not
a condition this glider can reach or would want to.

It matters because taking the largest lift coefficient over a range is the
obvious way to find a stall, and here it finds the wrong thing. Over 0–16° the
climbing branch has already overtaken the peak at the highest of these speeds,
so a global maximum reports the stall `{python} f"{worst:.1f}"`° late and at the
range boundary (@tbl-peaks) — a value that would move if the search window did,
which is the signature of the bug. The stall search now takes the **first**
turning point instead, which does not care where the window ends.

Nothing published moved: every entry that quotes a stall angle does so at
`{python} f"{rows[0][0]:.2f}"` or `{python} f"{rows[1][0]:.2f}"` m/s, where the
two methods happen to agree. The error only appears at the higher trim speed of
a heavier glider — which is exactly the case the next entry needed.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-peaks
#| tbl-cap: "The first peak against what a global maximum over 0–16° returns. They agree at the two lower speeds and disagree at the third."
import pandas as pd

pd.DataFrame({
    "speed [m/s]": [f"{r[0]:.2f}" for r in rows],
    "first peak": [f"{r[1]:.1f}°  (CL {r[2]:.3f})" for r in rows],
    "global max over 0–16°": [f"{r[3]:.1f}°  (CL {r[4]:.3f})" for r in rows],
    "local maxima found": [r[5] for r in rows],
}).style.hide(axis="index")
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-doublepeak
#| fig-cap: "Lift curve out to 24° at the three trim speeds. The filled marker is the stall — the first time lift stops rising. The cross is what a global maximum over 0–16° returns at the highest speed: the boundary of the search, on the post-stall branch."
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 4))

for (V, CL), colour in zip(curves.items(), ["C0", "C1", "C2"]):
    p = peaks(CL)
    ax.plot(a, CL, colour, lw=1.5, label=f"{V:.2f} m/s")
    ax.plot(a[p[0]], CL[p[0]], "o", color=colour, ms=7)
    g = int(np.argmax(CL[a <= 16]))          # what a global search would pick
    if abs(a[g] - a[p[0]]) > 0.5:
        ax.plot(a[g], CL[a <= 16][g], "x", color=colour, ms=9, mew=2)

ax.axvspan(0, 12, color="0.92", zorder=0)
ax.text(6, 0.05, "where this glider flies", ha="center", fontsize=8, color="0.45")
ax.set_xlabel(r"$\alpha$ [deg]"); ax.set_ylabel(r"$C_L$")
ax.set_xlim(0, 24); ax.grid(alpha=0.3); ax.legend()
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```
